title: Fabada Asturiana
subtitle: Asturian white bean stew with chorizo, morcilla and smoked pork
excerpt: Fabada is the great stew of Asturias: large, creamy faba beans simmered with chorizo, morcilla (blood sausage), and smoked pork until the broth is thick, porky, and deeply savoury. It is one of the most celebrated dishes in all of Spain -- hearty, filling, and impossible to rush.
sourceNotes: Fabada asturiana is the signature dish of Asturias, the mountainous region in the north of Spain. It is made with faba de La Granja beans -- a large, flat, pale bean grown in Asturias and protected by a designation of origin. Dried faba beans must be soaked for 12 hours. Dried cannellini beans are a practical substitute.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze in the broth. The beans may break down slightly on reheating.
recipe.batchNotes: Improves over 2 to 3 days. Make a large batch.

content.text: The beans must soak overnight. The pork needs to be smoked -- a smoked ham hock or smoked pancetta gives the broth its characteristic depth. Morcilla (blood sausage) can be replaced with black pudding. The stew should barely simmer, not boil -- a boiling fabada breaks the beans and makes a grey, grainy broth.

items.prepNote: dried, soaked overnight in cold water
in a piece if possible, or thick rashers

content.text: Drain the soaked {{cannellini-beans}} beans and put them in a large pot. Add enough cold water to cover by 5 cm. Add {{onion}} onion, {{garlic}} garlic, {{bay-leaves}} bay leaves, and {{extra-virgin-olive-oil}} oil. Bring slowly to a boil, skimming off any foam.

Add {{chorizo}} chorizo, {{black-pudding}} black pudding, and {{smoked-bacon}} smoked bacon to the pot. Add {{smoked-paprika}} smoked paprika and {{saffron}} saffron (if using). Reduce to the lowest possible simmer. Cook uncovered for 2 to 2.5 hours. The liquid should barely move.

When the beans are completely tender and the broth is thick, remove the chorizo, black pudding, and bacon. Slice into pieces and return to the pot. Season with {{salt-table}} salt. Serve in deep bowls with crusty bread.

items.symptom: The beans are firm after 2 hours
items.cause: Old dried beans take longer to cook, or they were not soaked long enough.
items.fix: Keep simmering. Old beans can take up to 3 hours. Never add salt until the beans are completely tender -- salt toughens the skins. Do not rush with a boil; it will break the beans without cooking them faster.

content.text: Fabada is the defining dish of Asturias, the green, mountainous region of northern Spain. It is eaten across the country but is most associated with the mining and farming communities of Asturias, where it was made to sustain people through cold winters. Fabada is also available in tins -- the Asturian tinned fabada is one of the most respected tinned foods in Spain.
